segments.text: Can a simple wire act like a magnet? Let us investigate.
Our circuit has a battery, switch, copper wire, resistor, and an ammeter connected in series.
Let us look inside the copper wire. We are enlarging a tiny part to see a teaching model of its particles.
The small blue dots are electrons. The copper-coloured spheres are copper ions, vibrating around fixed positions. These colours help us tell them apart.
With the switch OFF, electrons move randomly. There is no net flow around the circuit, so no magnetic field from a current in this wire.
Switch ON. Electrons now drift to the right. This net flow creates current and a magnetic field around the wire.
Electrons drift from negative to positive. Moving yellow arrows show conventional current in the opposite direction: positive to negative.
The green circles show the magnetic field around the wire. Their arrows show the field direction. The field remains while current flows.
Bring a magnetic compass near the wire. Its needle turns. That deflection helps us detect the magnetic field.
The ammeter reads half an ampere. Here, the compass deflection is about twenty-five degrees. Remember these starting readings.
Keep the wire and compass position the same. Now double the current. Compare the before and now readings on the ammeter and compass.

One ampere: the wire’s field is twice as strong at the same distance. More circles represent the stronger field. The needle turns from twenty-five to about forty-three degrees: about eighteen degrees further. The angle does not double.
Reduce the current again. The field weakens, and the compass needle turns back.

To summarize what we learned: moving charge produces current and a magnetic field. A compass detects it. More current means a stronger field. If current stops, the wireâ€™s field disappears; Earthâ€™s magnetic field remains.
